title: What is a Qubit?
summary: A qubit (quantum bit) is the fundamental unit of quantum information, analogous to the classical bit. Unlike a classical bit which is strictly 0 or 1, a qubit's state is a normalized vector in a two-dimensional complex Hilbert space: |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩, where α and β are complex probability amplitudes satisfying |α|² + |β|² = 1.
source: IBM Quantum Learning — Basics of Quantum Information

title: Computational Basis States |0⟩ and |1⟩
summary: The standard computational basis states are |0⟩ = [1, 0]ᵀ (ground state) and |1⟩ = [0, 1]ᵀ (excited state). They form an orthonormal basis for a single qubit. Any single-qubit quantum state can be expressed as a linear combination of these basis states.
source: IBM Quantum Learning — Single Qubit Systems

title: Quantum Superposition
summary: Superposition is the principle that a quantum state can be written as a linear combination of basis states: |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩. Crucially, a qubit in superposition is NOT 'both 0 and 1 at the same time'; it is in a single, well-defined quantum state whose complex amplitudes determine measurement probabilities via Born's rule.
source: IBM Quantum Learning — Multiple Systems and Superposition

title: Probability Amplitudes and Born Rule
summary: Probability amplitudes α and β are complex numbers with magnitude and phase. According to the Born rule, measuring in the standard basis yields outcome 0 with probability P(0) = |α|² and outcome 1 with probability P(1) = |β|². The normalization condition requires |α|² + |β|² = 1.
source: Qiskit Textbook — The Atoms of Computation

title: Measurement and Wavefunction Collapse
summary: Measurement extracts classical information from a quantum system and is fundamentally probabilistic. When a qubit in state α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ is measured in the computational basis, its state irreversibly collapses to |0⟩ (with probability |α|²) or |1⟩ (with probability |β|²), destroying superposition.
source: IBM Quantum Learning — Measurement in Quantum Circuits

title: The Bloch Sphere
summary: The Bloch sphere is a geometric representation of pure single-qubit states on the surface of a unit sphere: |ψ⟩ = cos(θ/2)|0⟩ + e^(iφ)sin(θ/2)|1⟩. The North pole represents |0⟩, South pole represents |1⟩, and the equator represents equal superpositions with differing relative phases φ.
source: Qiskit Documentation — Visualizing Quantum States

title: Hadamard Gate (H)
summary: The Hadamard gate creates equal superpositions from basis states: H|0⟩ = (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2 (state |+⟩) and H|1⟩ = (|0⟩ - |1⟩)/√2 (state |-⟩). Matrix: (1/√2)[[1, 1], [1, -1]]. Applying H twice returns the original state: H² = I.
source: IBM Quantum Learning — Single Qubit Gates

title: Pauli-X Gate (NOT Gate)
summary: The Pauli-X gate acts as the quantum bit-flip or NOT gate: X|0⟩ = |1⟩ and X|1⟩ = |0⟩. Matrix: [[0, 1], [1, 0]]. Geometrically on the Bloch sphere, X represents a π (180°) rotation around the X-axis.
source: IBM Quantum Learning — Single Qubit Gates

title: Pauli-Z Gate (Phase Flip Gate)
summary: The Pauli-Z gate acts as a phase-flip gate: Z|0⟩ = |0⟩ and Z|1⟩ = -|1⟩. Matrix: [[1, 0], [0, -1]]. It leaves state |0⟩ unchanged while flipping the relative phase of state |1⟩ by π radians (180°).
source: IBM Quantum Learning — Single Qubit Gates

title: Pauli-Y Gate
summary: The Pauli-Y gate performs both a bit-flip and a phase-flip with complex factor i: Y|0⟩ = i|1⟩ and Y|1⟩ = -i|0⟩. Matrix: [[0, -i], [i, 0]]. Corresponds to a π rotation around the Y-axis of the Bloch sphere.
source: IBM Quantum Learning — Single Qubit Gates

title: Phase Gates (S and T Gates)
summary: The S gate applies a π/2 (90°) phase rotation: S|1⟩ = i|1⟩ (matrix [[1, 0], [0, i]], S = √Z). The T gate applies a π/4 (45°) phase rotation: T|1⟩ = e^(iπ/4)|1⟩ (matrix [[1, 0], [0, e^(iπ/4)]], T = √S). Together with H, T provides universal quantum computation.
source: Qiskit Textbook — Single Qubit Gates

title: Controlled-NOT Gate (CNOT / CX)
summary: The CNOT (Controlled-X) gate is an entangling 2-qubit gate. If the control qubit is |1⟩, it flips the target qubit; if the control is |0⟩, the target is unchanged: CNOT|00⟩ = |00⟩, CNOT|01⟩ = |01⟩, CNOT|10⟩ = |11⟩, CNOT|11⟩ = |10⟩.
source: IBM Quantum Learning — Multiple Qubits and Entanglement

title: Quantum Entanglement
summary: Quantum entanglement occurs when two or more qubits share a joint state that cannot be factored into the tensor product of individual qubit states (|ψ⟩ ≠ |ψ_A⟩ ⊗ |ψ_B⟩). Measuring one entangled qubit instantaneously correlates the outcome of the other regardless of distance.
source: IBM Quantum Learning — Multiple Systems

title: Bell States (EPR Pairs)
summary: The four Bell states are maximally entangled two-qubit basis states: |Φ⁺⟩ = (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2, |Φ⁻⟩ = (|00⟩ - |11⟩)/√2, |Ψ⁺⟩ = (|01⟩ + |10⟩)/√2, |Ψ⁻⟩ = (|01⟩ - |10⟩)/√2. Created by applying H to qubit 0 followed by CNOT from qubit 0 to qubit 1.
source: Qiskit Textbook — Quantum Entanglement

title: Phase Kickback Effect
summary: Phase kickback is a quantum phenomenon where applying a controlled gate to a target qubit in an eigenstate (e.g. |-⟩ = (|0⟩ - |1⟩)/√2) 'kicks back' the eigenvalue phase shift onto the control qubit. It is the core mechanism enabling Deutsch-Jozsa, Grover, and Shor algorithms.
source: IBM Quantum Learning — Quantum Phase Kickback

title: Deutsch-Jozsa Algorithm
summary: The Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm determines with certainty whether a black-box boolean function f(x) is constant (same output for all inputs) or balanced (output 0 for half, 1 for half). Classically this requires up to 2^(n-1) + 1 evaluations; Deutsch-Jozsa solves it in exactly 1 quantum query via quantum parallelism and phase kickback.
source: IBM Quantum Learning — Fundamentals of Quantum Algorithms

title: Grover's Search Algorithm
summary: Grover's algorithm searches an unstructured database of N items in O(√N) evaluations compared to classical O(N), providing a quadratic speedup. It uses iterative amplitude amplification consisting of an oracle phase flip followed by an inversion-about-the-mean diffusion operator.
source: IBM Quantum Learning — Grover's Algorithm

title: Amplitude Amplification and Diffusion Operator
summary: Amplitude amplification geometrically rotates the quantum state vector toward the marked target state. The diffusion operator D = 2|s⟩⟨s| - I reflects all amplitudes across their average, turning a negative phase on the target state into constructively amplified probability while destructively canceling non-target states.
source: Qiskit Textbook — Grover's Algorithm

title: Quantum Parallelism and Interference
summary: Applying Hadamard gates across n qubits creates an equal superposition of all 2^n possible computational states. Quantum algorithms leverage constructive interference to amplify correct answers and destructive interference to cancel out incorrect answers.
source: IBM Quantum Learning — Basics of Quantum Information

title: Creating Circuits with Qiskit
summary: In Qiskit, quantum circuits are created via QuantumCircuit(num_qubits, num_clbits). Gates are applied sequentially (e.g. qc.h(0), qc.cx(0, 1)). Circuits can be simulated exactly using Statevector.from_instruction(qc) or sampled with measurement using the Sampler primitive.
source: Qiskit Documentation — Building Quantum Circuits
